stages.name: Automation and the labour market
stages.title: Current issue: automation substituting capital for labour
stages.sub: After this the student can explain why cheaper robots reduce jobs and why some displaced workers struggle to find new ones.

steps.q: A warehouse robot used to cost £80,000. New technology brings the price down to £20,000, while wages stay the same. What happens to the cost of using a robot instead of a worker?
steps.right: It falls, relative to hiring a worker
steps.wrong: It rises, relative to hiring a worker
steps.hint: The robot price dropped but wages did not move.
steps.pre: So the cost of the substitute factor has

steps.q: A delivery firm now finds robots much cheaper than before, relative to workers. What is it likely to do when planning its next batch of deliveries?
steps.wrong: Keep hiring the same number of workers
steps.hint: Firms tend to use more of whichever input has become relatively cheaper.

steps.q: After the firm switches to robots, what happens to the drivers whose jobs are removed?
steps.right: They lose their jobs and must look elsewhere
steps.wrong: They keep their same jobs at the firm
steps.hint: If robots now do the deliveries, what happens to the people who used to do them?

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 3 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Across the economy, capital keeps getting cheaper relative to labour, firms keep replacing workers with machines, and some displaced drivers have only ever driven vans with no skills that transfer to office jobs. What is this ongoing pattern called?
steps.right: Capital substituting for labour in the jobs market
steps.wrong: A temporary blip with no lasting effect on jobs
steps.hint: Put together the falling machine costs, the firms' choice, the workers left behind, and their lack of transferable skills.
